item.title: Not a game: Europol and partners target terrorist role-playing online
item.description: Europol’s European Union Internet Referral Unit (EU IRU) coordinated together with Spain a Referral Action Day targeting violent extremist and terrorist live action role-playing (LARPing) in online gaming environments. Specialised units from 16 countries participated in the action.

item.title: 5th EMPACT Hackathon leads to the detection of 51 potential victims
item.description: An international operation involving 40 experts and investigators from 20 countries has identified 51 potential victims of human trafficking, as well as five suspects. Held in Amsterdam from 23 to 25 September 2026, the fifth EMPACT Hackathon against the digital aspects of human trafficking brought together police officers, labour authorities and specialists in online investigations, supported by Europol and Eurojust.

item.title: Five TEFAF robbery suspects added to EU Most Wanted
item.description: As of 29 October 2026, five new fugitives, four men and one woman, have been added to the EU Most Wanted list. According to the Limburg Public Prosecutor's Office (Openbaar Ministerie) and the Dutch Police (Politie), all five suspects are involved in the European Fine Art Fair (TEFAF) robbery that took place on 28 June 2022 in Maastricht, the Netherlands.

item.title: 27 arrests and 248 potential victims identified in action week against labour exploitation
item.description: Europol, the European Labour Authority (ELA), and 34 participating countries today announced the results of an action week targeting human trafficking for labour exploitation. The operation, part of an EMPACT action led by Sweden, brought together police, border guards, labour and social security inspectorates, and tax authorities to crack down on exploitative practices in high-risk sectors such as agriculture, construction, cosmetic services, massage parlours, and hospitality.

item.title: Ordering violence from abroad: five suspects arrested in Spain, Morocco, and France
item.description:
Five suspects linked to the organisation and recruitment of serious violence have been arrested in Spain, Morocco, and France, in the latest results of the Operational Taskforce (OTF) GRIMM, coordinated by Europol.
The arrests in August and September target the upper levels of violence-as-a-service: those suspected of ordering attacks, finding perpetrators and coordinating crimes from abroad. Among those apprehended are fugitives featured on the EU Most Wanted website.

item.title: Android security advisory – November 2026 monthly rollup (AV26-1128)
7 tips for achieving defensive agility
item.description:
Defensive security agility reflects an organization’s potential to rapidly detect, adapt, and respond to evolving cyber threats and vulnerabilities without disrupting core operations. By abandoning static, rigid defense architectures, an agile defense plan emphasizes continuous iteration, automation, and cross-functional flexibility.

Defensive agility allows cybersecurity teams to rapidly adapt and respond to evolving threats while minimizing business disruption, says Anant Adya, an executive vice president at business and technology consulting firm Infosys. “As attack surfaces expand, organizations must prioritize risk quantification and identify vulnerabilities to strengthen their security posture and improve their ability to recover from attacks that are inevitable.”

Is your organization taking the steps needed to achieve a high degree of defensive agility? Read on to find out.

1. Establish a zero-trust baseline

Achieving defensive agility should begin with a zero-trust approach that continuously verifies access across users, devices, and applications, Adya advises. “An effective zero-trust strategy must be embedded into an organization’s technology framework and business lifecycle in order to build resilience and foster an organization-wide security mindset.”

As enterprises adopt AI, modernize applications, and operate across highly distributed environments, security must evolve from a protective afterthought into a business accelerant, Adya says. “By integrating zero trust into day-to-day operations and AI workflows, organizations can strengthen their ability to adapt to evolving threats while innovating faster, integrating acquisitions more securely, and scaling globally without accumulating architectural or operational debt.”

2. Modernize (and rationalize) your existing security infrastructure

Many large organizations are struggling to keep pace with emerging challenges because their systems are incredibly complex or filled with old software, custom code, and a mixture of disconnected security tools that can hinder containment speed, says Sharon Chand, cyber defense and resilience leader at Deloitte.

Chand advises CISOs to evaluate their existing infrastructure and technologies to consider how they’re currently responding to threats. Meanwhile, it’s important to streamline operations into a more integrated system. “Security organizations must also have access to AI-driven systems to detect and automate response to machine-speed attacks at the pace of adversaries,” she states.

3. Enlist AI where confidence is high and actions are reversible

Randy Gross, CISO at training and certification organization CompTIA, recommends deciding in advance which defensive actions are safe enough to happen without placing a human in the middle. “Locking an account, killing a session, or isolating a device should already be automated when confidence is high and the action is easy to reverse,” he says.

Review your strategy at least quarterly, but never equate a strategy review with operational governance, Gross warns. “In a medium-to-large enterprise, agents’ permissions and integrations may change frequently, so the guardrails around them must be continuous and automated,” he advises. “The CISO and team should also revisit their strategy when enough changes have been made to the point where risk has changed materially.”

Gross adds: “The strategy shouldn’t be just to put more AI in the SOC; it should be to reduce the latency between finding a threat and doing something useful about it.”

4. Forego higher walls in favor of dynamic, structural resilience

Defensive agility requires an enterprise system with the architectural capacity to absorb, isolate, and adapt to anomalous behavior without relying on human intervention, says Jatin Chopra, a senior software engineer at Microsoft. “It marks the transition from static perimeter defense — where you build higher walls — to dynamic, structural resilience where the environment itself constantly shifts to restrict threat propagation.”

Using an approach with sufficient capacity also detaches security from manual bottlenecking, Chopra says. “When defensive protocols are codified into the architecture rather than enforced by a review board, engineering teams can maintain high developer velocity while inherently restricting the attack surface.” It transforms security from a workflow tax into an automated platform capability, he states.

5. Beware bureaucracy that does not lead to decisive action

Stop treating your security strategy as an annual document process and begin viewing it as a loop that runs continuously utilizing data you trust, says Bob Maley, CISO at security-as-a-service provider Black Kite. Feed decisions to someone who actually has the authority to make rapid critical choices, he recommends.

Attackers are already highly vigilant, Maley warns. “When a new vulnerability opportunity lands on a Friday afternoon, nobody on a ransomware crew is waiting for a quarterly review to approve going after it,” he explains. “If your defense team needs a steering committee before it can react, the gap between their tempo and yours is where the breach lives.”

6. Embrace automation to free up human judgment

Most security teams I’ve worked with build static defenses, observes Timur Rakhmatullin, senior software engineer at Softline Solutions, a consulting and social media marketing services provider. “They set up rules, configure alerts, and write runbooks, but then something happens that doesn’t match the runbook and everyone freezes.”

Rakhmatullin believes that automation is essential. He runs automated security scans across 30-plus repositories using in-house tools. “The scans catch vulnerabilities, license issues, and other gaps,” Rakhmatullin explains. “But the key part is that any engineer can override a scan result, escalate it, or reclassify a finding in minutes.”

Still, automation does all the heavy lifting, Rakhmatullin says. “Humans make the judgment calls.”

7. Conduct regular ‘fire drills’

Rehearse ugly scenarios before they happen, suggests Chris McGlasson, founder of ClearStack Advisory, a fractional executive technology and AI strategy firm.

Know who patches, who tests, who talks to the business, and who has the authority to take something offline at 2 a.m., McGlasson says. “Write it down and run it twice a year,” he recommends. “The teams that do so treat incident response like a fire drill.” McGlasson adds that many CISOs risk disaster because they treat security like a research project instead of a fundamental initiative.

McGlasson points to the recent “Citrix meltdown,” a severe, ongoing security crisis affecting Citrix NetScaler ADC and NetScaler Gateway appliances, creating a mass wave of critical zero-day exploits. Citrix immediately warned IT administrators to patch their systems at once to address the issue.

As a result, the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, gave federal agencies a three-day patch window, while other organizations were left to create their own timeline, McGlasson says. He notes that the shops that handled this challenging event well weren’t always the ones with the best tools. “They were the ones that already knew who patches, who tests, and who calls the shots before the advisory ever dropped.”

Agility is a muscle, McGlasson observes. “You build it through repetition.”

item.title: Microsoft’s email security is unexpectedly blocking legitimate business mail
item.description:
Microsoft’s email filters meant to protect users from malicious messages appear to be rejecting legitimate ones.

Over the last few days, some mail sent to Microsoft consumer addresses have bounced if they did not publish a domain-based message authentication, reporting, and conformance (DMARC) record. This includes messages to Outlook, Hotmail, Live, and MSN.

The refusals began November 5 and are ongoing as of publication time . Microsoft did not announce a policy change and has not published a postmaster notice, service-health entry, or other blog post.

The issue may indicate that a policy change and a bug may both be in play, noted Frank Dickson of Dickson Research.

“Requiring every sending domain to prove it is who it says it is makes email safer,” he pointed out. “Doing it without notice, with an error message that points at the wrong problem, makes a mess.”

Intermittent sending issues

DMARC is meant to protect against spoofing, phishing, and business email compromise. Microsoft has had a rule in place since May 2025 requiring DMARC, but only from domains sending more than 5,000 messages a day to consumer mailboxes.

But as of November 5, mail from small, ordinary senders, rather than from bulk ones, have been bounced due to lack of DMARC, Sender Policy Framework (SPF), or DomainKeys Identified Mail (DKIM). Senders have been receiving Non-Delivery Reports (NDRs) citing 550 5.7.1 or 550 5.7.23 errors, but are doing so inconsistently; some messages are getting through while others are rejected.

For instance, one user reported this error message on Microsoft’s community forum:

Your message to @hotmail.com couldn’t be delivered.
hotmail.com couldn’t confirm that your message was sent from a trusted location.

Another user reported the same problem, adding: “Some emails work fine and others return errors with SPF failed.” Adding to the confusion, some bounced domains were reported to have working SPF, DKIM, and DMARC.

A Microsoft external staff moderator called it a “service degradation” currently under active investigation.

According to email security company MailRoute, enterprises can determine if their domain is impacted with this command on any terminal (replacing example.com with their domain): dig +short TXT _dmarc.example.com. A response starting with v=DMARC1 means there is a DMARC record; no reply means there isn’t, MailRoute said.

The fix is a single TXT record: v=DMARC1; p=none. This declares that a domain uses DMARC and asks receivers to send reports, but it tells them to take no action on failures, MailRoute explained.

DMARC meant to make impersonation difficult

DMARC relies on two foundational email authentication tools that must be active on a domain: SPF and DKIM.

SPF verifies whether the sending server’s IP address is allowed to send email on behalf of a domain, while DKIM adds a cryptographic signature to the message to prove it wasn’t altered along the way and actually belongs to the domain it says it is coming from.

DMARC checks the two, identifying whether the domain listed on the “from” address aligns with the validated domains. It ties those checks to the name the reader actually sees and tells receivers what to do with forgeries, Dickson explained.

“Without it, impersonating your domain is easy,” he said. “That is where a lot of phishing and business email compromise starts.”

But because Microsoft, at least to this point, has only required DMARC for larger senders, it is not standard across the board; many small senders reasonably concluded it did not apply to them, Dickson noted. This includes SMBs, nonprofits, schools, and professional practices such as law firms, accountants, and doctors’ offices running on domains that “someone set up years ago, and nobody has touched since.”

Larger organizations miss DMARC on secondary domains, regional domains, and the subdomains that their marketing and billing platforms send from for mundane reasons. No one owns the domain name system (DNS), and “people fear breaking legitimate mail sent by third parties,” Dickson said.

Quiet, inconsistent failure

As MailRoute pointed out, what makes this particular malfunction so dangerous is its inconsistency: The person who sent the message sees a bounce “full of acronyms, assumes a glitch, and moves on.” Meanwhile, the customer never knows a message was sent.

It fails quietly, which is “the bane of an email marketer’s existence,” Dickson said. Customers, patients, job applicants, and others use Hotmail, Outlook, Live, and MSN, and when invoices, password resets, appointment confirmations, and offer letters go missing, the customer thinks they’re being ignored, not necessarily that the message is not getting through.

The good news is that the failures are findable, he pointed out. Every rejection generated a bounce, and bounces are logged. Enterprises should search mail logs, email platforms’ bounce reports, and help desk tickets for entries citing “Message lacks SPF/DKIM/DMARC” since Nov. 5.

Then, resend what matters, time-sensitive transactional mail first.

From there, fix the cause by confirming that every domain sending mail as you publishes a DMARC record, Dickson advised. If one is missing, a basic monitoring record (p=none) stops these bounces without changing how anyone else treats your mail, as long as SPF or DKIM lines up with the From domain.

Microsoft 365 customers who never turned on DKIM for their own domains should do it now, he advised. “Do not rewrite SPF just because the bounce blames it,” he said. If your records are clean and mail still bounces, send the full bounce to Microsoft so it lands in the investigation.

However, a p=none record is “first base, not home plate,” he said. The goal is p=reject, which tells receivers to refuse anyone forging your name.

Inventory every service that sends email as you, Dickson advised: The CRM, the billing system, the HR platform, and the marketing tools. “Most organizations cannot produce that list,” he noted. “You cannot protect a domain when you do not know who is speaking for it.”

A signal of what is to come

While it remains to be seen what is causing this glitch, enterprises should make no mistake about where things are heading, Dickson said: DMARC will be enforced  for every sender. Google and Yahoo began requiring it of bulk senders in February 2024; Microsoft followed in May 2025.

“Requirements start with the big senders and then become the floor for everyone,” he said. “The rollout was botched, but the destination is not in doubt.” But while Microsoft has the destination right, “nobody should learn about a new rule from a bounce message.”

This article originally appeared on Computerworld.

item.title: SonicWall releases patches for 7 flaws in its firewalls, most involving unauthenticated access
item.description:
SonicWall on Monday updated its advisory about seven cybersecurity holes affecting its Gen 7 and Gen 8 firewalls, five of which allow unauthenticated remote attacks, to warn that it is aware of “potential” active exploitation of at least one of the bugs, CVE-2026-19868, a bypass of SAML authentication controls in its SonicOS SSL VPN service. 

And Frank Dickson, principal analyst at Dickson Research, pointed out that these flaws involve different SonicWall product lines to those recently reported.

“The July zero-day and the September holes hit SonicWall’s SMA 1000 remote access appliances,” he said. “This one hits SonicOS, the operating system on its Gen 7 and Gen 8 firewalls. The pattern has jumped product lines. That makes it a vendor issue, not a product issue. Credit where due: SonicWall flagged the exploitation report in its own advisory and the fix shipped with the disclosure.”

The seven vulnerabilities are: CVE-2026-107155, a permissive cross-domain policy vulnerability, with a CVSS score of 8.8; CVE-2026-107154, a session validation vulnerability, also with a CVSS score of 8.8; CVE-2026-82308, a pre-authentication heap buffer overflow vulnerability in SSL-VPN, with a CVSS score of 7.5; CVE-2026-19868, an authentication enforcement vulnerability via alternate authentication methods, with a CVSS score of 7.1; CVE-2026-77708, a pre-authentication stack buffer overflow vulnerability in TACACS+, with a CVSS score of 5.9; CVE-2026-77709 , a pre-authentication heap buffer overflow vulnerability in TACACS+, with a CVSS score of also 5.9; and CVE-2026-19703, a weak password hashing hole with a CVSS score of 5.2.

SonicWall only provided a workaround for one of the bugs, CVE-2026-19868; it involves disabling or deleting any active LDAP, RADIUS, and TACACS+ authentication server configured on the firewall.

A ‘mixed bag’

Dickson said the newly reported holes are a mixed bag.

“SonicWall’s advisory rates its SAML bypass, CVE-2026-19868, a 7.1, below two 8.8 management interface flaws,” Dickson said. “Yet it is the one CISA added to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog the same day SonicWall disclosed it. SonicWall describes ‘potential exploitation’ but CISA says active. I would listen to CISA.”

The bug lets anyone holding valid credentials for another login method, such as a local account or LDAP, skip SAML and the MFA that rides on it, he noted, adding “companies moved their VPNs to SAML precisely so every login passes through the identity provider and its MFA prompt. This flaw breaks that promise.”

Some of the other authentication holes are potentially less severe, however.

“Three are pre-authentication buffer overflows whose stated impact is denial of service. They knock the VPN offline but they do not open it,” Dickson said. “The two 8.8 flaws work only under specific conditions. None of the six is known to be exploited. They matter, [but] they are not the headline.”

Could be combined

Sav Wheeler, malware research engineer at Malwarebytes, added that even though some of these holes do not appear to be especially serious on their own, they could be combined to be much more dangerous. 

“These scattered vulnerabilities at various stages of the authentication process combine to form a pathway where an attacker can bypass authentication almost entirely to penetrate a system and steal credentials,” Wheeler said. “The weak password hashing is a cherry on top for attackers that have already gained an initial foothold.”

He sees CVE-2026-19868 as “the biggest individual vulnerability” because the potential MFA bypass through alternative authentication means that “the entire trust boundary of MFA could be effectively nonexistent even when an organization depends on it for security.”

He noted, however, that although the attacker does need valid credentials for an alternate authentication method for this to work, “otherwise it requires little effort and resources to gain access, as they’re not compromising the MFA itself. Combined with the use of IP addresses for validation (CVE-2026-107154), which itself provides little security, this is a serious failure of authentication policy to ensure a user is who they claim to be.”

Sanchit Vir Gogia, chief analyst at Greyhound Research, said that the biggest danger is when SAML sits atop older directory logins that stay live. 

“Remote access is the lifeblood of a distributed business, and one stolen directory password now reaches it. CISOs who rolled out SAML to end password-only access have cause to feel let down. SonicWall owes them a full account of how the second path stayed open.”

A vendor risk management issue

These continuing SonicWall vulnerabilities are a real issue, although the September and October flaws sit in another product, Gogia said. “Those hit the SMA1000 remote-access gateway, while this advisory covers SonicOS firewalls. But thirteen of SonicWall’s twenty entries in CISA’s exploited list carry the flag for known ransomware use, the highest share among eight edge vendors.”

Dickson noted that the next steps for enterprise CISOs are trickier because the fault here might lie less with a vendor than with the product category itself.

“The internet-facing VPN appliance is the Achilles’ heel of the perimeter, whoever builds it,” he pointed out. “Swapping vendors swaps one heel for another. The pattern should change how CISOs deploy the edge, not just whose logo is on it. Ask SonicWall whether these are new bugs or the same bug classes coming back.”

However Erik Avakian, technical counselor at Infotech, said he was less willing to let SonicWall off the hook that easily.

“Any vendor can and is generally going to experience vulnerabilities, but when we see repeated critical security issues affecting the same vendor that represent a pattern, particularly involving authentication and internet-facing infrastructure, it raises legitimate questions about their secure development practices, quality assurance, and the effectiveness of their own internal vulnerability management processes,” Avakian said. “At some point, this becomes more than just an individual vulnerability management issue. It becomes a vendor risk management issue.”

He noted that CISOs need to evaluate whether the frequency and severity of these vulnerabilities are creating an unacceptable level of recurring exposure for their organization. “That doesn’t automatically mean replacing SonicWall products, but it does require holding the vendor accountable for improvement and to demonstrate their ability to address the underlying problems,” he said.

Additional preventive measures

In addition, Dickson suggested other ways CISOs can protect themselves in light of these new holes, beyond the obvious step of patching them.

“List every way the VPN can authenticate a user: local accounts, LDAP, RADIUS, and TACACS+. Delete what you do not need, especially leftover local admin and service accounts. Rotate passwords on every non-SAML account that remains,” he advised. “Compare VPN logins against identity provider sign-ins. A VPN session with no matching SAML sign-in is your red flag. Look back as far as your logs go, since SonicWall has not said when exploitation began. And take the management interface off the open internet.”

item.title: When everything is a threat, nothing feels safe
item.description:
When you leave home, you lock the door. When you get into the car, you fasten your seat belt. These are familiar safety habits. We understand their purpose, know how to perform them and rarely need to stop and think about them.

Our digital lives are different. We shop, bank, work and keep in touch with family and friends online, often without clear signs of where a danger begins or which precaution matters most. We receive a steady stream of warnings about new scams, stolen credentials, data breaches and software vulnerabilities. The messages vary in urgency, but many seem to demand our immediate attention.

The result can be an uncomfortable contradiction: information intended to make us safer can also leave us overwhelmed and less willing to act.

In conversations with people inside and outside the technology field, I keep hearing variations of the same concerns. There is a new scam every week, and no way to keep up. If major companies can be breached, how can an individual protect themselves? Almost anything done online seems risky.

These are reasonable questions. As a cybersecurity professional, I believe our response should go beyond repeating that threats exist. We need to help people understand which risks are relevant, what they can do about them and where their responsibility ends.

When a warning becomes background noise

There are good reasons to monitor the threat landscape. Criminals adapt their techniques, fraud schemes evolve and vulnerabilities sometimes require urgent remediation. Ignoring those developments is not a sensible strategy.

But a threat’s existence is not the same as a person’s or organization’s exposure to it. A vulnerability described as critical does not necessarily create the same level of risk for every business. The answer depends on which products are in use, whether affected systems are exposed, what safeguards are already in place and the potential business impact.

A critical flaw in technology that an organization does not use may be worth noting without requiring emergency action. A less dramatic issue affecting a business-critical, internet-facing service could deserve immediate attention. The headline alone cannot make that distinction.

Yet headlines are often how people encounter cybersecurity. When warnings arrive without context, prioritization or practical guidance, they compete for a limited amount of attention. What should be exceptional starts to feel routine. An alert that genuinely requires action may disappear into the noise.

There is a meaningful difference between staying informed and feeling compelled to remain on high alert every moment of the day.

Security fatigue is not simply a lack of interest

Researchers have a name for part of this experience: security fatigue. In a 2016 qualitative study, researchers at the US National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) interviewed 40 everyday computer users about security and privacy. Signs of fatigue appeared in 25 interviews, even though fatigue was not the study’s initial focus.

Participants described frustration with repeated requirements and advice, along with feelings of resignation and diminished control. The researchers connected these experiences with decision avoidance, choosing the easiest option available, and disregarding protective guidance. The study was small and qualitative, so it should not be treated as a measure of how widespread fatigue is today. Its value lies in explaining behavior that security teams may otherwise label as carelessness.

When someone dismisses yet another warning, they may not be indifferent to security. They may simply have lost the ability to tell what matters, what is urgent and what action is expected of them.

This distinction matters for security leaders. If every message is marked urgent, we should not be surprised when urgency stops working. More warnings are not automatically better communication.

Replace headline volume with decision criteria

I do not believe people need to memorize every new phishing technique or follow every vulnerability disclosure to practice sound digital security. Nor is it sustainable for security teams to treat every issue as equally important.

A better approach starts with three questions whenever a new alert appears:

1. Does this affect me or my organization? Is the alert about a service, device, account or process I use or oversee?

2. Does it require action now? Is there credible guidance and a concrete reason for urgency, or is this general information about a possible threat?

3. What is the most effective action available to me? Should I install an update, verify an unusual request through another channel, enable a safeguard or notify the appropriate team?

This is not a guarantee of safety. It is a way to separate useful information from noise and preserve attention for decisions that matter.

For individuals, a consistent baseline is more valuable than trying to recognize the scam of the week: keep devices and applications updated, use long and unique passwords with a password manager, enable multifactor authentication and verify requests that demand immediate action or sensitive information. These habits are easy to describe, even if implementing them sometimes requires help.

For organizations, the equivalent is a risk-based process that connects alerts to actual assets, exposure, business priorities and clear owners. A security bulletin should answer who is affected, what the organization knows, what needs to happen and by when. When no action is required, saying so is also useful.

The burden cannot rest entirely on users

It would be unfair to finish this discussion by giving people another long list of obligations. If staying secure requires every employee to interpret technical warnings, navigate confusing settings and make the correct choice every time, the design of the system is part of the problem.

Organizations and technology providers should make secure behavior easier by default. That includes sensible protective settings, automated updates where appropriate, effective filtering, straightforward reporting channels and clear instructions when a real decision is necessary. It also means preparing for mistakes through detection, response and recovery rather than assuming flawless human behavior.

NIST’s work on human-centered cybersecurity makes a similar case: systems and guidance should account for people’s actual needs, capabilities and limitations. The goal is to make safe actions easier to take in practice, not merely to issue more instructions.

Security leaders can put that principle to work by reviewing the warnings employees receive. Are several teams sending overlapping messages about the same threat? Do alerts explain the action and its owner? Are we asking employees to solve problems that technical control could prevent? Can people report a suspicious message without fearing blame?

These questions recognize that user behavior matters, but it always takes place within a system that can support or undermine good decisions.

Build awareness through confidence

I want security awareness to treat people as partners, not as the weakest link to be frightened into compliance. Good risk communication should explain why something matters, whom it affects and what realistic next step is available. It should also be able to say when there is no reason to panic.

Confidence does not mean assuming nothing will go wrong. It means understanding the most relevant risks, knowing which protections are in place and knowing where to turn when something unusual happens.

We should therefore be careful about how we measure awareness. The number of alerts distributed, or training messages delivered tells us little about whether people can act on what they have learned. I would rather ask a more demanding question: After receiving our guidance, are people better equipped to make a sound decision?

If the answer is no, we need to change how we communicate cybersecurity.

Awareness should not be about frightening people. It should provide knowledge, a sense of control and practical ways to act.

item.title: Anthropic sharpens AI coding and security capabilities with Mythos 5.2
item.description:
Anthropic has introduced Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2, claiming significant improvements in handling complex software engineering tasks while cutting API prices by 20% compared with the previous versions.

Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 share the same underlying model but have different safeguards. Fable is broadly available, while direct access to Mythos is restricted to vetted cybersecurity and life sciences organizations to limit potential misuse.

The models are both priced at $8 per million input tokens and $40 per million output tokens, down from $10 and $50, respectively. Anthropic said the newer versions can generate output up to 30% faster than their predecessors.

The company reported substantial gains in coding performance. Fable 5.2 scored 49.1% on the FrontierCode 2.0 benchmark at its Xhigh effort setting, compared with 32.4% for Fable 5.1. The benchmark assesses whether maintainers of open-source projects would accept AI-generated changes to their code.

Performance and costs could entice enterprises

The models’ improved performance and lower prices could make long-running AI agents viable for software migrations and scientific research, according to Lian Jye Su, chief analyst at Omdia. Higher task completion rates could further reduce deployment costs, he said.

Anthropic said Fable 5.2 at its “High effort” setting achieved a coding benchmark score comparable to Opus 5.5 at its highest setting, at roughly half the cost per task. The comparison suggests that Fable could be more economical for some demanding assignments, although the savings would depend on the workload and effort setting.

“Anthropic has cut the price of a token, not the price of a thought,” said Sanchit Vir Gogia, chief analyst at Greyhound Research. He urged CIOs to treat AI processing effort as a budget consideration and measure costs against successfully completed tasks.

Anthropic also recommends Opus 5.5 for most coding and knowledge work, with Fable and Mythos intended for more demanding assignments.

Reliability challenges persist

In an internal experiment, an Anthropic engineer tasked Fable 5.2 with building a prototype operating system. The model coordinated more than 1,000 subagents over eight days and produced software that could boot on a laptop.

Su said the improvements bring enterprises closer to highly autonomous software development, although widespread deployment will depend on addressing persistent operational limitations.

“Reliability remains an issue without human supervision,” Su said.

Coordinating multiple AI agents across enterprise tools and internal teams also remains difficult, he added. Organizations will need to monitor agent activity and run these systems in appropriately isolated environments. Critical changes should remain subject to human approval, with sufficient visibility into agent behavior to support audits.

Pareekh Jain, CEO of Pareekh Consulting, said complex legacy systems and the need to meet business requirements could limit how much software development enterprises can delegate to AI agents.

Faster vulnerability discovery raises concerns

Anthropic said Mythos 5.2 identified 89.6% of vulnerabilities in its internal CVE Rediscovery evaluation, compared with 78.3% for Mythos 5.1.

Conducted against 1,829 previously disclosed vulnerabilities, the test assessed whether models could independently rediscover flaws in software snapshots taken before the vulnerabilities were fixed. The company said Mythos 5.2 was also better at reproducing vulnerabilities and developing fixes.

Anthropic has restricted direct access to Mythos 5.2 through its verification programs. However, Claude Enterprise customers can use the model’s vulnerability detection capabilities through Claude Security without joining those programs, the company said.

According to Su, “Mythos 5.2 shifts the balance towards defenders in controlled enterprise settings.”

Jain, however, cautioned that advances in AI-powered vulnerability discovery could also help attackers identify software weaknesses more quickly. “This creates an AI-powered race between attackers and defenders,” he said.

Data retention raises compliance questions

Anthropic said customers eligible for zero data retention can continue using Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 under those arrangements, while other customers face 30-day retention for safety monitoring.

The company has also introduced Enterprise Frontier Safeguards, currently in private beta, which allows automated safety monitoring to run on prompts and responses stored within customers’ infrastructure.

Gogia said data retention requirements could outweigh the benefits of lower API prices for regulated enterprises. He urged procurement teams to obtain written confirmation of zero-retention arrangements before deploying the models for sensitive workloads.

The article originally appeared on InfoWorld.

item.title: Qubole supply chain attack exposed AWS, Entra ID, and Okta credentials
item.description:
An attacker has abused AWS cross-account IAM roles to access multiple customer environments, steal data, and harvest credentials in a supply-chain attack that ran between October 14 and October 26.

Researchers from Wiz, working with Sentra and Mandiant, said they observed an attacker using IAM credentials for Qubole’s AWS account to assume roles in customer environments.

The compromised credentials allowed the attacker to access customer AWS accounts that had previously established cross-account access permissions with Qubole. The access was used to enumerate cloud resources, retrieve secrets and configuration data, download files from Amazon S3, and test credentials belonging to affected organizations.

Sentra, which initially identified suspicious activity across several customer environments, said the campaign affected dozens of Qubole customers. The attacker was said to have exploited integrations that remained trusted even after some organizations had stopped using the platform.

Attackers used Qubole’s AWS credentials

Qubole integrations rely on cross-account Identity and Access Management (IAM) roles. Customers typically create roles that allow identities belonging to Qubole’s AWS account to assume them, with an External ID serving as an additional check against unauthorized access.

The attacker had credentials that could satisfy this requirement.

Wiz said the first suspicious activity was observed on October 14, when an IP address associated with Mullvad VPN attempted to assume customer integration roles from AWS account 805246085872, which Qubole uses for its platform operations. The requests used an IAM user identified as AIDA3W7DIFLYOLTK63SFS.

Most of the activity that came later originated from an OVH-hosted VPS, 57.129.54[.]120. The attacker also began using a second IAM identity associated with Qubole’s AWS account on October 18, alongside another Mullvad VPN address.

All malicious role-assumption requests identified by Wiz included the required External ID and succeeded. Many of the targeted roles had seen no legitimate Qubole activity during October, but their permissions remained active.

After gaining access, the attacker enumerated cloud resources, including S3 buckets, databases, EC2 instances, security groups and IAM identities. The intruder also accessed AWS Secrets Manager, Systems Manager Parameter Store and Lambda function configurations to retrieve credentials and other sensitive information.

Attackers stole data, and hosted a suspicious Linux image

The attacker used the assumed roles to download data from Amazon S3, enumerating accessible buckets and objects before retrieving their contents. In some instances, Wiz said, entire buckets were downloaded in individual sessions.

Credentials discovered in the compromised environments were subsequently tested using TruffleHog, a secrets-scanning tool. These included AWS access keys, Microsoft Entra ID service principal credentials and Okta OAuth client credentials.

Sentra reported identifying more than 100 passwords and keys read within minutes, alongside thousands of additional credential records contained in downloaded files. The company also said the attacker performed no write operations in the observed environments, suggesting an operation focused on data theft.

Wiz also found a bootable Linux ISO image, named “sso_agent.iso,” hosted on the attacker’s OVH infrastructure. The image collects system information, communicates with the server over TCP port 23458, and can execute remotely supplied shell commands. Its configuration suggests it may have been designed to target Windows systems, the researchers said in a blog post.

Wiz, however, did not find any deployments of the image and could not confirm whether it had been used against victims.

The campaign has not been attributed to a known threat group.

Tightening integrations and third-party access will help

Wiz recommends that organizations using Qubole review AWS CloudTrail records dating back to October 1, 2026, across all accounts containing integration roles. Investigators should look for suspicious AssumeRole activity originating from Qubole’s AWS account, particularly requests from non-AWS infrastructure and IAM identities identified in the disclosure.

Subsequent activity involving Secrets Manager, Parameter Store, Lambda and S3 should also be investigated, Wiz noted. Other recommendations include removing unused third-party integrations and narrowing trust policies to specific vendor IAM principals rather than allowing an entire external AWS account to assume a role. Organizations should also restrict role assumption to documented vendor network ranges using AWS source IP or VPC endpoint conditions.
